error_modes.label: Knowledge of the daily assignment exercises

texts.0: SP, due to incomplete study of the daily assignment, could not state the sequence, the entry parameters or the completion criteria of the exercises briefed for the sortie. SP did not know in detail all exercises given as daily assignment, so the IP had to teach the profile from the beginning at the pre-flight briefing. Two assigned exercises had to be demonstrated in flight before SP could attempt them and the planned repetitions were not completed.
texts.1: SP, due to a superficial review of the daily assignment, recalled the exercises only in outline and produced entry parameters only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP. Knowledge of the assigned exercises stayed at the minimum acceptable limit and the sequence had to be restated verbally before each maneuver. SP flew the whole profile, but the delay in recall left no time for the last set of repetitions.
texts.2: SP, due to studying the daily assignment late in the preparation, hesitated on the entry parameters of two exercises at the pre-flight briefing. SP identified the gap without IP input, went back to the assignment sheet and restated the correct sequence and completion criteria before the walk-around. The profile was then flown as planned and no exercise had to be re-briefed in flight.
texts.3: SP knew in detail all exercises given as daily assignment and stated their sequence, entry parameters and completion criteria without hesitation. Answers at the pre-flight briefing were prompt and accurate and the same knowledge was applied in flight without prompting. The post-flight briefing confirmed correct understanding of every assigned exercise.
texts.4: SP knew every exercise of the daily assignment in exceptional detail, including the reason behind each parameter and the errors most commonly associated with it. SP briefed the complete profile to the IP without notes and correctly linked each exercise to the preceding sorties of the syllabus. Every question at the post-flight briefing was answered accurately and with the correct reference.
texts.marginal: SP knew all exercises given as daily assignment to the required standard, but answers on the last exercises of the profile were slower and less detailed than on the first ones. The trend indicates that preparation is concentrated on the early part of the assignment. SP is expected to study the whole assignment with the same depth so that recall is uniform across the complete profile.

texts_at.0: SP worked through knowledge of the daily assignment, with the IP demonstrating the technique first, a first exposure to this task at this stage of the syllabus. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard, and SP is expected to carry more of the task independently at the next opportunity.
texts_at.1: SP knew the daily assignment exercises inside the code 1 band, entry parameters produced only after repeated prompting on two exercises. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to study the whole assignment with the same depth so recall is uniform across the complete profile.
texts_at.2: SP knew the daily assignment exercises inside the code 2 band, correcting a gap on the entry parameters of two exercises found and restated before the walk-around. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to review the assignment sheet once more before the briefing so no gap needs correcting there.
texts_at.3: SP knew in detail all exercises given as daily assignment and stated their sequence, entry parameters and completion criteria without hesitation, with answers on the last exercises of the profile a little slower than the first. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to bring the same pace to those last exercises.

texts_above.1: SP knew the daily assignment exercises, with the entry parameters of two exercises recalled only on the second attempt. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP identified a gap in the entry parameters of two exercises without IP input, returned to the assignment sheet and restated the correct sequence and completion criteria before the walk-around. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good study of the daily assignment.
texts_above.3: SP knew in detail all exercises given as daily assignment and stated their sequence, entry parameters and completion criteria without hesitation, with prompt and accurate answers at the pre-flight briefing confirmed again at the post-flight briefing. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good study of the daily assignment.
texts_above.4: SP knew every exercise of the daily assignment in exceptional detail, including the reason behind each parameter and the errors most commonly associated with it, briefing the complete profile to the IP without notes. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent study of the daily assignment.

error_modes.label: Flight Manual, Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and aeronautical publications

texts.0: SP, due to not having reviewed the Flight Manual and the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, quoted an operating limit incorrectly and could not locate the applicable paragraph when asked. SP did not know in detail the publications required for the flight, including AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications (MAIP, maps). The IP had to state the correct limits and read the procedure aloud before the sortie could be briefed.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete study of the Flight Manual and the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, produced the correct limit only after the IP indicated the chapter to be opened. Knowledge of the required publications remained at the minimum acceptable limit and every reference had to be confirmed verbally by the IP. SP finally quoted the correct paragraph, but the search delayed the pre-flight briefing.
texts.2: SP, due to relying on memory instead of the current publication, misstated one value of the Flight Manual limits at the pre-flight briefing. SP recognized the error without IP intervention, opened the manual and gave the correct value together with its paragraph within a few seconds. The remaining questions on the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications were answered accurately.
texts.3: SP knew in detail the Flight Manual, the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications (MAIP, maps) and used them with confidence. Limits, normal procedures and the applicable rules were quoted correctly and with the right reference at both briefings. No answer required correction by the IP.
texts.4: SP used all handbooks related to the flight with complete confidence, quoting limits and procedures verbatim together with chapter and paragraph. SP also explained how the Flight Manual limits and the AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 rules applied to the specific conditions of the sortie and cross-checked the information against the aeronautical publications. Knowledge exceeded the level expected at this stage of the syllabus.
texts.marginal: SP knew the Flight Manual and the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual to the required standard, but answers drawn from AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications were noticeably slower and more general. The trend shows that study is concentrated on the aircraft handbooks and not on the regulatory and navigation publications. SP is expected to study all handbooks required by BD 3-1/HATC with the same depth so that every reference is used with equal confidence.

texts_at.0: SP worked through the required manuals and publications, with the IP talking through each step as it was flown, the supporting technique still being built at this point. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage, and SP is expected to rely less on the IP's assistance as the item is repeated.
texts_at.1: SP knew the Flight Manual and the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual inside the code 1 band, the correct limit produced only after the IP indicated the chapter. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to study all handbooks required by BD 3-1/HATC with the same depth so every reference is used with equal confidence.
texts_at.2: SP knew the Flight Manual and the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual inside the code 2 band, correcting one misstated limit recognized without IP intervention. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to confirm figures against the current publication rather than from memory.
texts_at.3: SP knew in detail the Flight Manual, the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications and used them with confidence, with answers drawn from the regulatory and navigation publications a little more general than the aircraft handbook answers. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to bring those answers to the same precision.

texts_above.1: SP knew the Flight Manual and the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, with one limit not recalled from memory on the first question. SP corrected the trend after a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a misstated Flight Manual value without IP intervention, opened the manual and gave the correct value together with its paragraph within a few seconds. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound manual and publication knowledge.
texts_above.3: SP knew in detail the Flight Manual, the A/C Techniques and Procedures Manual, AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications and used them with confidence, quoting limits, normal procedures and applicable rules correctly with the right reference at both briefings. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed manual and publication knowledge.
texts_above.4: SP used all handbooks related to the flight with complete confidence, quoting limits and procedures verbatim together with chapter and paragraph and explaining how the Flight Manual limits applied to the specific conditions of the sortie. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional manual and publication knowledge.

error_modes.label: Meteorological principles and the morning meteorological briefing

texts.0: SP, due to not identifying the weather threats of the mission during preparation, could not interpret the forecast presented at the morning meteorological briefing. SP did not demonstrate knowledge of the meteorological principles required to follow the briefing and could not state the effect of the reported cloud base and wind on the planned profile. The IP had to explain the weather picture and reassign the working area before the sortie could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to reviewing the weather only in outline, followed the morning meteorological briefing with difficulty and answered on the expected conditions only after repeated questions by the IP. Knowledge of meteorological principles stayed at the minimum acceptable limit, since every consequence for the profile had to be pointed out verbally. SP flew the planned sortie, but the assessment of the weather threats was made for SP rather than by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to preparing the weather picture from a single source, initially misjudged the trend of the reported cloud base for the working area. SP identified the discrepancy without IP input, went back to the forecast and stated the correct expected conditions and their effect on the profile before start. The morning meteorological briefing was otherwise followed without problem and no weather item had to be re-explained.
texts.3: SP demonstrated knowledge of meteorological principles and attended the morning meteorological briefing without problem. SP interpreted the reported and forecast conditions correctly and stated their effect on the working area, the traffic pattern and the alternate before the flight. The weather assessment made at the briefing matched the conditions actually encountered.
texts.4: SP interpreted the morning meteorological briefing in exceptional detail, explaining the physical mechanism behind the forecast conditions and their expected development during the sortie window. SP anticipated the effect of the reported wind and cloud base on the working area and on the traffic pattern and proposed the corresponding adjustment to the profile. The in-flight conditions confirmed the assessment made before the flight.
texts.marginal: SP attended the morning meteorological briefing without problem and interpreted the current conditions correctly, but answers on the forecast development during the sortie window were general and lacked the underlying principle. The trend indicates that preparation covers the reported weather but not its expected evolution. SP is expected to study meteorological principles further so that the forecast can be interpreted with the same confidence as the current observation.

texts_at.0: SP worked through the morning meteorological briefing, with the IP providing hands-on guidance on the controls, the sequence still new to SP at this stage of training. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet, and SP is expected to manage more of the sequence unaided on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP followed the morning meteorological briefing inside the code 1 band, expected conditions answered only after repeated questions from IP. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to study meteorological principles further so the forecast can be interpreted with the same confidence as the current observation.
texts_at.2: SP followed the morning meteorological briefing inside the code 2 band, correcting an initial misjudgment of the cloud base trend identified without IP input. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to cross-check the forecast against a second source rather than relying on one.
texts_at.3: SP demonstrated knowledge of meteorological principles and attended the morning meteorological briefing without problem, interpreting the reported conditions correctly, with answers on the forecast development a little more general than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to bring that same precision to the forecast development.

texts_above.1: SP followed the morning meteorological briefing, with the expected conditions for the sortie recalled only after a second question. The adjustment followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP identified a discrepancy in the reported cloud base trend without IP input, went back to the forecast and stated the correct expected conditions and their effect on the profile before start. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady grasp of meteorological principles.
texts_above.3: SP demonstrated knowledge of meteorological principles and attended the morning meteorological briefing without problem, interpreting the reported and forecast conditions correctly and stating their effect on the working area, the traffic pattern and the alternate before the flight. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate grasp of meteorological principles.
texts_above.4: SP interpreted the morning meteorological briefing in exceptional detail, explaining the physical mechanism behind the forecast conditions and anticipating the effect of the reported wind and cloud base on the working area. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary grasp of meteorological principles.

error_modes.label: Aerodynamics knowledge applied to in-flight situations

texts.0: SP, due to not having studied the aerodynamics of the assigned maneuvers, could not explain theoretically the situations encountered during the flight. SP gave an incorrect explanation of the relation between angle of attack, load factor and stall speed and could not connect it to the maneuvers flown. The IP had to teach the theory at the post-flight briefing and the corresponding exercises were programmed for repetition.
texts.1: SP, due to a memorized rather than understood treatment of the theory, explained the aerodynamics of the maneuvers only after the IP built the answer step by step with successive questions. Knowledge remained at the minimum acceptable limit, since no situation encountered in flight was explained without verbal cueing. SP finally reached the correct explanation, but only with continuous IP guidance at the post-flight briefing.
texts.2: SP, due to confusing two effects of airspeed on control response, gave an incomplete explanation of the aircraft behaviour observed in one maneuver. SP identified the error unprompted, corrected the explanation and linked it correctly to the airspeed and load factor of that maneuver. The remaining situations encountered during the flight were explained theoretically without IP assistance.
texts.3: SP demonstrated aerodynamics knowledge sufficient to explain theoretically the situations encountered during the flight. The explanation of the behaviour of the aircraft in each assigned maneuver was accurate, prompt and correctly linked to airspeed, angle of attack and load factor. No part of the theory had to be corrected by the IP.
texts.4: SP explained the aerodynamics of every situation encountered during the flight with exceptional accuracy and used the theory to predict the behaviour of the aircraft before the maneuvers were flown. SP correctly related control response, angle of attack and load factor to the errors observed in the sortie and proposed the corresponding technique correction. The depth of the explanation exceeded the standard expected at this stage.
texts.marginal: SP explained the situations encountered during the flight to the required standard, but the explanations remained descriptive and needed a second attempt whenever the question moved from the maneuver to the underlying principle. The trend suggests that theory is learned per maneuver rather than as a set of principles. SP is expected to consolidate aerodynamics knowledge so that any in-flight situation can be explained directly from first principles.

texts_at.0: SP worked through applied aerodynamics knowledge, with the IP walking through the sequence step by step, the pace of the item still unfamiliar at this point. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance, and SP is expected to need less of that guidance on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP explained theoretically the situations encountered during the flight inside the code 1 band, the correct explanation reached only after the IP built it with successive questions. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to consolidate aerodynamics knowledge so any in-flight situation can be explained directly from first principles.
texts_at.2: SP explained theoretically the situations encountered during the flight inside the code 2 band, correcting an incomplete explanation of one maneuver identified unprompted. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to link airspeed, angle of attack and load factor together on the first attempt at the explanation.
texts_at.3: SP demonstrated aerodynamics knowledge sufficient to explain theoretically the situations encountered during the flight, with the explanation of one maneuver needing a second pass before it was complete. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to bring that explanation to the same standard as the rest on the first pass.

texts_above.1: SP explained theoretically the situations encountered during the flight, with one explanation incomplete on the first attempt. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified an incomplete explanation of one maneuver unprompted, corrected it and linked it correctly to the airspeed and load factor of that maneuver, explaining the remaining situations without IP assistance. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable applied aerodynamics knowledge.
texts_above.3: SP demonstrated aerodynamics knowledge sufficient to explain theoretically the situations encountered during the flight, with each explanation accurate, prompt and correctly linked to airspeed, angle of attack and load factor. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good applied aerodynamics knowledge.
texts_above.4: SP explained the aerodynamics of every situation encountered during the flight with exceptional accuracy and used the theory to predict the behaviour of the aircraft before the maneuvers were flown. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior applied aerodynamics knowledge.

error_modes.label: Airport traffic procedures and flight planning

texts.0: SP, due to omitting the risk assessment of the planned sortie, did not know the airport traffic procedures for the runway in use and produced a flight plan that was not executable. SP could not state the departure and recovery routing, the pattern altitude or the applicable radio calls. The IP had to plan the flight and brief the traffic procedures in full before the sortie could be flown.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete assessment of the risks of the planned profile, stated the airport traffic procedures only in part and completed the flight plan after repeated verbal corrections by the IP. Knowledge of the procedures and of the planning data stayed at the minimum acceptable limit, with the recovery routing supplied by the IP. SP flew the sortie as planned, but only after the plan had been corrected item by item at the briefing.
texts.2: SP, due to using the traffic procedures of the reciprocal runway during the initial planning, briefed an incorrect pattern entry for the runway in use. SP detected the error without IP input, checked the aeronautical publications and corrected the entry, the pattern altitude and the associated radio calls before taxi. The rest of the flight plan was complete and no further correction was required.
texts.3: SP knew the airport traffic procedures and had sufficient knowledge to plan the flight. Departure, recovery and pattern procedures for the runway in use were stated correctly and the flight plan was complete, realistic and consistent with the assigned profile. The plan was executed as briefed and required no correction by the IP.
texts.4: SP knew the airport traffic procedures in exceptional detail and planned the flight including the fuel, time and airspace constraints of each phase. SP identified in advance the traffic and airspace threats of the sortie and briefed the corresponding decision points and the alternative recovery. The plan proved fully executable and covered situations that were not required at this stage of the syllabus.
texts.marginal: SP knew the airport traffic procedures and planned the flight to the required standard, but the planning of the recovery phase was thinner than that of the departure and needed a second look before it was complete. The trend shows that preparation is weighted toward the first part of the sortie. SP is expected to plan every phase of the flight, up to and including the recovery, with the same level of detail.

texts_at.0: SP worked through airport traffic procedures and flight planning, with the IP prompting each action verbally as the item developed, this being SP's first presentation of the item. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point, and SP is expected to take over more of the sequence without prompting next time.
texts_at.1: SP knew the airport traffic procedures and had sufficient knowledge to plan the flight inside the code 1 band, the flight plan completed only after repeated verbal corrections. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to plan every phase of the flight, up to and including the recovery, with the same level of detail.
texts_at.2: SP knew the airport traffic procedures and had sufficient knowledge to plan the flight inside the code 2 band, correcting a pattern entry briefed for the wrong runway after checking the publications unaided. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to confirm the runway in use before the entry is briefed rather than after.
texts_at.3: SP knew the airport traffic procedures and had sufficient knowledge to plan the flight, with departure, recovery and pattern procedures stated correctly, and the planning of the recovery phase a little thinner than that of the departure. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to plan the recovery phase to the same depth as the departure.

texts_above.1: SP knew the airport traffic procedures and had sufficient knowledge to plan the flight, with two items of the flight plan incomplete on the first pass. SP corrected the trend after a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP identified an incorrect pattern entry briefed for the wrong runway without IP input, checked the aeronautical publications and corrected the entry, the pattern altitude and the associated calls before taxi. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured airport traffic procedures and flight planning.
texts_above.3: SP knew the airport traffic procedures and had sufficient knowledge to plan the flight, with departure, recovery and pattern procedures for the runway in use stated correctly and the flight plan complete, realistic and consistent with the assigned profile. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise airport traffic procedures and flight planning.
texts_above.4: SP knew the airport traffic procedures in exceptional detail and planned the flight including the fuel, time and airspace constraints of each phase, identifying the traffic and airspace threats in advance. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate airport traffic procedures and flight planning.

texts.0: SP, due to not having studied air medicine and flight physiology, could not interpret the physiological conditions and flight effects encountered during the sortie. SP gave an incorrect description of the symptoms and of the corrective action for the effects of sustained load factor and could not state the associated aircrew limitations. The IP had to teach the subject at the post-flight briefing before the profile could be repeated.
texts.1: SP, due to superficial preparation on flight physiology, described the effects encountered in flight only after the IP listed the symptoms and asked for each one in turn. Knowledge of air medicine remained at the minimum acceptable limit and no physiological condition was interpreted without verbal cueing. SP reached the correct interpretation, but only through repeated IP prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to mixing the symptoms of two physiological effects, gave an incomplete initial interpretation of the sensations reported during the maneuvers. SP corrected the interpretation without IP input, identified the effect correctly and stated the associated countermeasure and its limits. The remaining questions on air medicine and flight physiology were answered accurately.
texts.3: SP demonstrated knowledge of air medicine and flight physiology and interpreted correctly all the physiological conditions and flight effects encountered during the sortie. Symptoms, causes and countermeasures were stated accurately and promptly at the post-flight briefing. No part of the interpretation required correction by the IP.
texts.4: SP interpreted every physiological condition and flight effect of the sortie in exceptional detail, including the onset mechanism, the aggravating factors and the tolerance limits of the aircrew. SP related the effects experienced in flight to the specific maneuvers and load factors flown and stated the preventive measures for the next sortie. Knowledge of air medicine exceeded the level expected at this stage.
texts.marginal: SP interpreted the physiological conditions encountered in flight to the required standard, but answers on the preventive and physical countermeasures were general and lacked the associated limits. The trend indicates that study covers the symptoms but not the management of the effects. SP is expected to study air medicine and flight physiology further so that both the recognition and the countermeasures are stated with the same confidence.

texts_at.0: SP worked through air medicine and flight physiology, with the IP demonstrating the technique first, a first exposure to this task at this stage of the syllabus. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard, and SP is expected to carry more of the task independently at the next opportunity.
texts_at.1: SP described the effects encountered in flight inside the code 1 band, each condition interpreted only after the IP asked for it in turn. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to study air medicine and flight physiology further so recognition and countermeasures are stated with equal confidence.
texts_at.2: SP described the effects encountered in flight inside the code 2 band, correcting an incomplete interpretation of two mixed symptoms recognized without IP input. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to separate similar symptoms on the first pass rather than after they have been mixed.
texts_at.3: SP demonstrated knowledge of air medicine and flight physiology and interpreted correctly all the physiological conditions and flight effects encountered during the sortie, with answers on the preventive countermeasures a little more general than on the symptoms. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to bring the countermeasures to the same precision.

texts_above.1: SP described the effects encountered in flight, with one condition left unstated until asked for by name. The adjustment followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP corrected an incomplete interpretation of the sensations reported during the maneuvers without IP input, identifying the effect correctly and stating the associated countermeasure and its limits. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good air medicine and flight physiology knowledge.
texts_above.3: SP demonstrated knowledge of air medicine and flight physiology and interpreted correctly all the physiological conditions and flight effects encountered during the sortie, stating symptoms, causes and countermeasures accurately and promptly at the post-flight briefing. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good air medicine and flight physiology knowledge.
texts_above.4: SP interpreted every physiological condition and flight effect of the sortie in exceptional detail, including the onset mechanism, the aggravating factors and the tolerance limits of the aircrew. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent air medicine and flight physiology knowledge.

error_modes.label: Sea and land survival and SAR rescue procedures

texts.0: SP, due to not having reviewed the survival material, was not aware of the sea and land survival procedures or of the rescue procedures from SAR means. SP could not state the actions after landing in the water, the use of the survival equipment carried or the signals used with the rescue means. The IP had to cover the whole subject at the briefing and the item was programmed for re-examination.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete preparation on survival, listed the land survival actions only in part and stated the sea procedures after repeated prompting by the IP. Awareness of the rescue procedures from SAR means stayed at the minimum acceptable limit, with the sequence of signals supplied verbally by the IP. SP produced the correct answers, but no part of the subject was recalled independently.
texts.2: SP, due to treating sea and land survival as one common procedure, gave an incorrect initial answer on the actions immediately after water entry. SP recognized the error unprompted, separated the two procedures correctly and stated the sea survival sequence and the associated equipment without assistance. The rescue procedures from SAR means were then described accurately.
texts.3: SP was aware of both sea and land survival procedures and of the rescue procedures from SAR means. The sequence of actions, the use of the survival equipment and the signals used with the rescue means were stated correctly and without hesitation. No item of the subject required correction by the IP.
texts.4: SP described the sea and land survival procedures and the rescue procedures from SAR means in exceptional detail, including the equipment carried, its limitations and the priorities in each environment. SP adapted the procedure to the terrain and sea conditions of the planned working area and stated the corresponding communication and signalling plan. The knowledge shown exceeded the standard expected at this stage of the syllabus.
texts.marginal: SP was aware of both sea and land survival procedures to the required standard, but the description of the rescue procedures from SAR means was less structured and had to be reordered before it was complete. The trend shows that study covers the survival phase but not the recovery phase. SP is expected to review the SAR rescue procedures so that the whole sequence, from the emergency to the pick-up, is stated with the same confidence.

texts_at.0: SP worked through survival and SAR rescue procedures, with the IP talking through each step as it was flown, the supporting technique still being built at this point. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage, and SP is expected to rely less on the IP's assistance as the item is repeated.
texts_at.1: SP was aware of the sea and land survival procedures and the SAR rescue procedures inside the code 1 band, the sequence of signals supplied verbally before it was recalled. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to review the SAR rescue procedures so the whole sequence, from the emergency to the pick-up, is stated with the same confidence.
texts_at.2: SP was aware of the sea and land survival procedures and the SAR rescue procedures inside the code 2 band, correcting an initial answer that treated the two environments as one procedure. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to separate the two procedures from the first answer rather than after a correction.
texts_at.3: SP was aware of both sea and land survival procedures and of the rescue procedures from SAR means, stating the sequence of actions, the survival equipment and the signals correctly, with the description of the rescue procedures a little less structured than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to structure that description as clearly as the rest.

texts_above.1: SP was aware of the sea and land survival procedures and the SAR rescue procedures, with one signal sequence out of order on the first recall. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP corrected an initial answer that had treated sea and land survival as one procedure without prompting, separating the two correctly and stating the sea survival sequence and equipment unaided. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound survival and SAR procedures knowledge.
texts_above.3: SP was aware of both sea and land survival procedures and of the rescue procedures from SAR means, stating the sequence of actions, the use of the survival equipment and the signals used with the rescue means correctly and without hesitation. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed survival and SAR procedures knowledge.
texts_above.4: SP described the sea and land survival procedures and the rescue procedures from SAR means in exceptional detail, including the equipment carried, its limitations and the priorities in each environment, adapting the procedure to the planned working area. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional survival and SAR procedures knowledge.

error_modes.label: Chair flying of the sortie during mission specific study

texts.0: SP, having omitted the chair fly required by mission specific study, did not visualize the manoeuvres and did not mentally review the checklists and the specific tasks before flight. At the pre-flight briefing SP could not state the profile without reading it, and in flight every manoeuvre entry had to be set up by the IP. Two exercises already demonstrated in a previous sortie had to be demonstrated again and the sortie objectives were not met.
texts.1: SP chair flew only the first part of the sortie, so the visualization of the later manoeuvres and the mental review of the checklists were left incomplete. Preparation stayed at the minimum acceptable limit and the IP had to prompt verbally the entry sequence of the last three exercises. All manoeuvres were flown, but each one started late and one planned repetition was lost.
texts.2: SP chair flew the sortie quickly and without visualizing the transitions between manoeuvres, so the order of the last two exercises was recalled incorrectly at the briefing. SP identified the omission without IP input, chair flew the remaining profile again before step and then stated the sequence correctly. No manoeuvre had to be re-briefed in flight.
texts.3: SP chair flew the complete sortie, visualizing every manoeuvre and technique and mentally reviewing the checklists and the specific tasks. The profile was briefed in the correct order without notes and every exercise was entered without prompting. The cockpit flow in flight followed the sequence rehearsed on the ground.
texts.4: SP chair flew the sortie in exceptional detail, visualizing each manoeuvre together with its entry parameters, its completion criteria and the errors most commonly associated with it. The checklists and the specific tasks were rehearsed aloud, including the radio calls of each phase. The whole profile then ran without a single prompt and the time gained allowed two additional repetitions.
texts.marginal: SP chair flew the sortie to the required standard, but the visualization covered the manoeuvres only and not the checklists or the transitions between exercises. Preparation was sufficient for the profile flown, yet the trend shows rehearsal limited to the parts SP considers difficult. SP is expected to chair fly the complete sortie, checklists and specific tasks included.

texts_at.0: SP practiced chair-flying the sortie, with the IP providing hands-on guidance on the controls, the sequence still new to SP at this stage of training. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet, and SP is expected to manage more of the sequence unaided on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP chair flew the sortie during mission specific study inside the code 1 band, the entry sequence of the last exercises prompted verbally before it was recalled. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to chair fly the complete sortie, checklists and specific tasks included.
texts_at.2: SP chair flew the sortie during mission specific study inside the code 2 band, correcting an incorrectly recalled sequence of the last two exercises identified without IP input. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to visualize the transitions between maneuvers as carefully as the maneuvers themselves.
texts_at.3: SP chair flew the complete sortie, visualizing every maneuver and technique and mentally reviewing the checklists and the specific tasks, with the profile briefed in the correct order and only one exercise entered a little less smoothly than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to enter that exercise as smoothly as the others.

texts_above.1: SP chair flew the sortie during mission specific study, with the entry sequence of the last exercises slower to recall than the rest. SP corrected the trend after a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified an incorrectly recalled sequence without IP input, chair flew the remaining profile again before step and then stated the sequence correctly. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady chair-flying preparation.
texts_above.3: SP chair flew the complete sortie, visualizing every maneuver and technique and mentally reviewing the checklists and the specific tasks, briefing the profile in the correct order without notes with every exercise entered without prompting. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate chair-flying preparation.
texts_above.4: SP chair flew the sortie in exceptional detail, visualizing each maneuver together with its entry parameters, completion criteria and the errors most commonly associated with it, rehearsing the checklists and radio calls aloud. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary chair-flying preparation.

error_modes.label: Pre-sortie review of the individual manoeuvres in the Flight Manual and this manual

texts.0: SP came to the briefing without having reviewed the individual manoeuvres in the appropriate sections of the Flight Manual and of the Techniques and Procedures Manual. SP could not state the published technique of two manoeuvres of the profile and used entry parameters recalled from an earlier sortie. The IP had to open both manuals at the briefing table and teach the technique before the profile could be flown.
texts.1: SP reviewed the manoeuvres of the sortie in the Techniques and Procedures Manual only and did not open the corresponding sections of the Flight Manual. Knowledge of the published technique remained at the minimum acceptable limit and the IP had to correct verbally the entry parameters of two manoeuvres. The sortie was flown as planned, but the references were quoted by the IP and not by SP.
texts.2: SP reviewed the manoeuvres late in the preparation and confused the published technique of two similar exercises at the start of the briefing. SP asked for a short pause, checked both sections in the manuals and restated the correct technique before the walk-around. The rest of the briefing and the sortie required no further correction of references.
texts.3: SP reviewed every manoeuvre of the sortie in the appropriate sections of the Flight Manual and of the Techniques and Procedures Manual before flight. Entry parameters, sequence of actions and completion criteria were stated with the correct reference and without hesitation. The technique applied in flight matched the published one throughout the profile.
texts.4: SP reviewed every manoeuvre in both manuals and quoted the paragraph supporting each entry parameter and each limitation used. The published technique had also been compared with the errors debriefed in the previous sorties and the corrections were briefed accordingly. Every question at the post-flight briefing was answered with the correct reference.
texts.marginal: SP reviewed the manoeuvres of the sortie in both manuals to the required standard, but the review of the new exercises was clearly deeper than that of the exercises already flown. Answers on the repeated manoeuvres were correct, yet slower and given without reference. SP is expected to review all manoeuvres of the profile with the same depth, repeated exercises included.

texts_at.0: SP worked through the pre-sortie manual review, with the IP walking through the sequence step by step, the pace of the item still unfamiliar at this point. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance, and SP is expected to need less of that guidance on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP reviewed the manoeuvres of the sortie in the Flight Manual and the Techniques and Procedures Manual inside the code 1 band, entry parameters of two manoeuvres corrected verbally before they were recalled. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to review all manoeuvres of the profile with the same depth, repeated exercises included.
texts_at.2: SP reviewed the manoeuvres of the sortie in the Flight Manual and the Techniques and Procedures Manual inside the code 2 band, correcting a confusion between two similar exercises identified at the start of the briefing. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to distinguish similar exercises before the briefing begins rather than during it.
texts_at.3: SP reviewed every manoeuvre of the sortie in the appropriate sections of the Flight Manual and of the Techniques and Procedures Manual before flight, stating entry parameters, sequence and completion criteria with the correct reference, with the review of one repeated exercise a little thinner than the new ones. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to review that exercise with the same depth.

texts_above.1: SP reviewed the manoeuvres of the sortie in the Flight Manual and the Techniques and Procedures Manual, with the entry parameters of two manoeuvres not recalled on the first pass. The adjustment followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a confusion between two similar exercises at the start of the briefing, checked both sections in the manuals and restated the correct technique before the walk-around. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable pre-sortie manual review.
texts_above.3: SP reviewed every manoeuvre of the sortie in the appropriate sections of the Flight Manual and of the Techniques and Procedures Manual before flight, with entry parameters, sequence of actions and completion criteria stated with the correct reference and without hesitation. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good pre-sortie manual review.
texts_above.4: SP reviewed every manoeuvre in both manuals and quoted the paragraph supporting each entry parameter and limitation used, comparing the published technique with the errors debriefed in previous sorties. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior pre-sortie manual review.

error_modes.label: Study time devoted to possible alternate missions

texts.0: SP devoted study time to the primary mission only and none to the possible alternate missions. When the weather imposed the change of profile, SP could not state the manoeuvres, the working area or the recovery of the alternate mission. The IP had to brief the alternate sortie from the beginning on the ground and the planned objectives were not met.
texts.1: SP studied the alternate mission in outline only, so its manoeuvres were recalled after repeated prompting by the IP. Preparation for the alternate profile stayed at the minimum acceptable limit and the change of mission cost about ten minutes of additional briefing. The alternate sortie was flown, but its last exercise was not completed within the fuel available.
texts.2: SP arrived having prepared the primary mission only and hesitated when the IP raised the possible alternate profile. SP identified the gap without prompting, reviewed the alternate mission and its manoeuvres before step and briefed it correctly. The change of profile in flight then required no additional instruction.
texts.3: SP focused the study on the primary mission and still devoted time to the possible alternate missions. When the profile was changed, SP briefed the alternate mission, its manoeuvres and its working area without prompting. The sortie continued with no loss of time and with all planned repetitions completed.
texts.4: SP studied the primary mission in depth and had also prepared the two most likely alternate missions, each with its airspace, fuel plan and recovery. The change of profile was proposed by SP with the reasoning stated before the IP raised it. The alternate sortie was then flown complete with every planned repetition.
texts.marginal: SP devoted time to the possible alternate missions to the required standard, but the preparation covered their manoeuvres and not their airspace or fuel plan. Knowledge was sufficient for a change of profile briefed by the IP. SP is expected to prepare the alternate missions as completely as the primary one.

texts_at.0: SP worked through preparation for the alternate mission, with the IP prompting each action verbally as the item developed, this being SP's first presentation of the item. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point, and SP is expected to take over more of the sequence without prompting next time.
texts_at.1: SP devoted study time to the possible alternate missions inside the code 1 band, the manoeuvres recalled only after repeated prompting by IP. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to prepare the alternate missions as completely as the primary one.
texts_at.2: SP devoted study time to the possible alternate missions inside the code 2 band, correcting a gap in the alternate profile identified without prompting before step. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to review the alternate mission during the same pass as the primary rather than afterward.
texts_at.3: SP focused the study on the primary mission and still devoted time to the possible alternate missions, briefing the alternate mission, its manoeuvres and its working area without prompting when the profile changed, with the alternate airspace covered a little less than its manoeuvres. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to bring the airspace study to the same depth.

texts_above.1: SP devoted study time to the possible alternate missions, with the manoeuvres of one alternate mission recalled more slowly than the primary mission. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified a gap in the alternate mission preparation without prompting, reviewed the alternate mission and its manoeuvres before step and briefed it correctly. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured preparation for the alternate mission.
texts_above.3: SP focused the study on the primary mission and still devoted time to the possible alternate missions, briefing the alternate mission, its manoeuvres and its working area without prompting when the profile was changed and continuing the sortie with no loss of time. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise preparation for the alternate mission.
texts_above.4: SP studied the primary mission in depth and had also prepared the two most likely alternate missions, each with its airspace, fuel plan and recovery, proposing the change of profile before the IP raised it. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate preparation for the alternate mission.

error_modes.label: A-A-B-C-D-E-F method: boldface stated before the situation is analyzed
error_modes.source: technique:1.21 TABLETOP AND STAND-UP EMERGENCY PROCEDURES (EPS)

texts.0: SP, at the stand-up emergency procedure, started stating boldface steps before establishing A/C control and before analyzing the situation. The FEVER check was not used and the boldface selected did not correspond to the malfunction given. The IP stopped the exercise and taught the A-A-B-C-D-E-F sequence from the beginning before it could be attempted again.
texts.1: SP moved from A/C control directly to the boldface and analyzed the situation only after the IP asked what the indications were. Application of the A-A-B-C-D-E-F method stayed at the minimum acceptable limit and each analysis item had to be prompted verbally. The correct boldface was finally stated, but only after that prompting.
texts.2: SP began to state the boldface before the analysis of the situation was complete. SP stopped without IP input, returned to the FEVER check and only then stated and verbally executed the applicable boldface. The remaining steps of the method followed in the correct order.
texts.3: SP applied the A-A-B-C-D-E-F method in order, stabilizing the A/C, analyzing the situation with the FEVER check and only then stating and executing the boldface. Each step was verbalized before it was executed and no boldface was applied before the analysis supported it. The exercise was carried to a safe landing without correction.
texts.4: SP applied the method in order and explained why each analysis item excluded or supported the malfunction before any boldface was stated. Time stands still was used to question the IP on the systems concerned and the boldface selected was justified from the indications obtained. The whole exercise was completed without a single prompt and with correct reasoning throughout.
texts.marginal: SP kept the A-A-B-C-D-E-F order to the required standard, but the analysis preceding the boldface was noticeably shorter on the second emergency than on the first. The correct boldface was still selected each time. SP is expected to keep the analysis complete on every emergency, including those that appear familiar.

texts_at.0: SP practiced the A-A-B-C-D-E-F method, with the IP demonstrating the technique first, a first exposure to this task at this stage of the syllabus. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard, and SP is expected to carry more of the task independently at the next opportunity.
texts_at.1: SP applied the A-A-B-C-D-E-F method in order inside the code 1 band, each analysis item prompted verbally before the boldface was stated. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to keep the analysis complete on every emergency, including those that appear familiar.
texts_at.2: SP applied the A-A-B-C-D-E-F method in order inside the code 2 band, correcting a boldface begun before the analysis of the situation was complete on one emergency. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to complete the FEVER check before any boldface is stated, not only after stopping mid-sequence.
texts_at.3: SP applied the A-A-B-C-D-E-F method in order, stabilizing the A/C, analyzing the situation with the FEVER check and only then stating and executing the boldface, with the analysis on the second emergency noticeably shorter than on the first. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to keep that analysis as complete as the first.

texts_above.1: SP applied the A-A-B-C-D-E-F method in order, with one analysis item worked through slowly before the boldface was stated. SP corrected the trend after a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP stopped before completing a boldface begun early, returned to the FEVER check and only then stated and verbally executed the applicable boldface, with the remaining steps following in order. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady application of the A-A-B-C-D-E-F method.
texts_above.3: SP applied the A-A-B-C-D-E-F method in order, stabilizing the A/C, analyzing the situation with the FEVER check and only then stating and executing the boldface, with each step verbalized before it was executed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate application of the A-A-B-C-D-E-F method.
texts_above.4: SP applied the method in order and explained why each analysis item excluded or supported the malfunction before any boldface was stated, using time stands still to question the IP on the systems concerned. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary application of the A-A-B-C-D-E-F method.

error_modes.label: Return to A/C control after each boldface and each checklist
error_modes.source: technique:1.21 TABLETOP AND STAND-UP EMERGENCY PROCEDURES (EPS)

texts.0: SP executed the boldface and then the cleanup checklist without ever referring back to A/C control. SP did not state how the control stick, the rudder and the PCL would be used to compensate for the reduced thrust when the PCL was moved below 60 %, and the flight condition described was left unflyable. The IP had to interrupt and rebuild the exercise from the A/C control step.
texts.1: SP referred back to A/C control only after the IP asked what the A/C was doing at the end of the checklist. The link between each checklist and A/C control stayed at the minimum acceptable limit and the compensation required after moving the PCL below 60 % was described only when prompted. The exercise was completed, but the return to A/C control was never initiated by SP.
texts.2: SP passed from the boldface to the next checklist without first checking A/C control. SP identified the omission without IP input, returned to the A/C control step, stated the stick, rudder and PCL inputs needed after the PCL reduction and then continued with the checklists.
texts.3: SP referred back to A/C control after every boldface and every checklist and stated the stick, rudder and PCL inputs required to keep the A/C stabilized. After the engine failure during flight boldface the A/C was described trimmed at 125 KIAS, and the reduction of the PCL below 60 % was accompanied by the correct compensation for the reduced thrust. The exercise progressed through all checklists with the A/C under control at each step.
texts.4: SP referred back to A/C control after every boldface and checklist and each time stated the trim, the airspeed and the power setting at which the A/C would be left. The compensation after moving the PCL below 60 % was described with the exact stick, rudder and PCL inputs and with the resulting rate of descent from the 125 KIAS glide. The whole exercise was flown mentally with the A/C stabilized at every step and without any prompting.
texts.marginal: SP referred back to A/C control after each boldface and checklist to the required standard, but the description became shorter as the exercise progressed and the last checklist was followed by a general statement only. Control was still accounted for at every step. SP is expected to state the specific stick, rudder and PCL inputs after every checklist, including the last ones.

texts_at.0: SP practiced returning to aircraft control after each boldface, with the IP talking through each step as it was flown, the supporting technique still being built at this point. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage, and SP is expected to rely less on the IP's assistance as the item is repeated.
texts_at.1: SP referred back to A/C control after each boldface and checklist inside the code 1 band, the compensation required after moving the PCL described only when prompted. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to state the specific stick, rudder and PCL inputs after every checklist, including the last ones.
texts_at.2: SP referred back to A/C control after each boldface and checklist inside the code 2 band, correcting an omission identified without IP input before returning to the A/C control step. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to check A/C control before moving to the next checklist rather than after.
texts_at.3: SP referred back to A/C control after every boldface and every checklist and stated the stick, rudder and PCL inputs required to keep the A/C stabilized, with the description becoming a little shorter as the exercise progressed. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to keep that description as full at the end as at the start.

texts_above.1: SP referred back to A/C control after each boldface and checklist, with the compensation required after moving the PCL left undescribed on the first pass. The adjustment followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified an omission without IP input, returned to the A/C control step, stated the stick, rudder and PCL inputs needed after the PCL reduction and then continued with the checklists. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable return to aircraft control after each step.
texts_above.3: SP referred back to A/C control after every boldface and every checklist and stated the stick, rudder and PCL inputs required to keep the A/C stabilized, describing the aircraft trimmed at 125 KIAS after the engine failure boldface with the correct compensation after each reduction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good return to aircraft control after each step.
texts_above.4: SP referred back to A/C control after every boldface and checklist and stated the trim, the airspeed and the power setting at which the A/C would be left, describing the compensation with the exact stick, rudder and PCL inputs each time. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior return to aircraft control after each step.

error_modes.label: Verification of the boldface effect and search for the next applicable boldface
error_modes.source: technique:1.21 TABLETOP AND STAND-UP EMERGENCY PROCEDURES (EPS)

texts.0: SP executed the boldface and moved on without verifying whether it had done what it was intended to do. No second FEVER check was performed and SP never asked whether another boldface applied, so the immediate engine start following the engine failure during flight was never considered. The IP had to stop the exercise and teach the boldface loop.
texts.1: SP verified the effect of the boldface only after the IP asked what the engine indications were, and the question of a further applicable boldface was also raised by the IP. The boldface loop stayed at the minimum acceptable limit and had to be driven by prompting throughout. The correct follow-on boldface was eventually stated.
texts.2: SP started the cleanup checklist without a second FEVER check after the boldface. SP stopped without IP input, performed the FEVER check, confirmed fuel flow steady within 10 pph and ITT within limits, asked whether another boldface applied and then continued. No further omission followed in the exercise.
texts.3: SP performed a second FEVER check after every boldface and stated whether the boldface had produced the intended result. SP then asked whether another boldface applied and stayed in that loop until none remained. The transition to the cleanup checklists was made only after the loop was closed.
texts.4: SP ran the complete FEVER check after each boldface and stated for every item, fluctuating fuel flow beyond 10 pph, excessive ITT, visual indications, erratic operation and roughness, whether it had improved or not. Where the indications did not change, SP explained what that implied for the malfunction before moving to the next applicable boldface. The whole boldface loop was closed without prompting.
texts.marginal: SP verified the effect of each boldface and searched for the next applicable one to the required standard, but the second FEVER check after the last boldface was abbreviated to the fuel flow alone. The conclusion drawn was still correct. SP is expected to run the complete FEVER check after every boldface and not only after the first.

texts_at.0: SP practiced verifying the boldface effect, with the IP providing hands-on guidance on the controls, the sequence still new to SP at this stage of training. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet, and SP is expected to manage more of the sequence unaided on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP verified the effect of the boldface and searched for the next applicable one inside the code 1 band, the boldface loop driven by prompting throughout. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to run the complete FEVER check after every boldface and not only after the first.
texts_at.2: SP verified the effect of the boldface and searched for the next applicable one inside the code 2 band, correcting an omitted second FEVER check identified without IP input. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to run the FEVER check immediately after each boldface rather than after starting the cleanup.
texts_at.3: SP performed a second FEVER check after every boldface and stated whether the boldface had produced the intended result, asking whether another boldface applied and staying in that loop until none remained, with the last check abbreviated to fuel flow alone on one occasion. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to run that check in full as well.

texts_above.1: SP verified the effect of the boldface and searched for the next applicable one, with the loop slower than the briefed pace throughout. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP stopped without IP input before an omitted second FEVER check, performed the check, confirmed fuel flow and ITT within limits, asked whether another boldface applied and then continued. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured verification of the boldface effect.
texts_above.3: SP performed a second FEVER check after every boldface and stated whether the boldface had produced the intended result, then asked whether another boldface applied and stayed in that loop until none remained, transitioning to the cleanup checklists only once it was closed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise verification of the boldface effect.
texts_above.4: SP ran the complete FEVER check after each boldface and stated for every item whether it had improved or not, explaining what an unchanged indication implied for the malfunction before moving to the next applicable boldface. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate verification of the boldface effect.

error_modes.label: Declaring the emergency with a plan (nature, time to landing, souls on board, briefing)
error_modes.source: technique:1.21 TABLETOP AND STAND-UP EMERGENCY PROCEDURES (EPS)

texts.0: SP declared the emergency before any game plan existed and could not tell ATC the nature of the emergency, the time to landing, the souls on board or the plan of action. Neither the pattern to be flown nor the way the A/C would be stopped had been decided. The IP had to teach the content of the declaration and the recovery plan before the exercise could continue.
texts.1: SP declared the emergency and passed the nature of the emergency only, adding the time to landing, the souls on board and the plan of action after the IP prompted each item in turn. The content of the declaration stayed at the minimum acceptable limit. The pattern was stated, but the method of stopping the A/C was given only on request.
texts.2: SP declared the emergency with an incomplete call that omitted the souls on board and the plan of action. SP identified the omission without IP input, restated the complete call to ATC and added the pattern to be flown and the intention to stop on the runway for emergency ground egress.
texts.3: SP established the game plan first and then declared, giving ATC the nature of the emergency, the time to landing, the souls on board and the briefing of the plan of action. The pattern to be flown and the way the A/C would be stopped after landing were both stated. No item of the declaration had to be prompted.
texts.4: SP declared with a complete plan and added the fuel remaining, the field selected and the point at which the plan would be changed if the situation deteriorated. The call to ATC contained the nature of the emergency, the time to landing, the souls on board and a concise briefing of the plan of action. The requirement for ground emergency services and the intentions after stopping were also briefed.
texts.marginal: SP declared the emergency with a plan to the required standard, but the briefing of the plan of action was less specific than the rest of the call and the stopping intention was expressed in general terms. All required items were nevertheless passed. SP is expected to state the pattern type and the method of stopping the A/C with the same precision as the other items.

texts_at.0: SP practiced declaring the emergency with a plan, with the IP walking through the sequence step by step, the pace of the item still unfamiliar at this point. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance, and SP is expected to need less of that guidance on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP declared the emergency with a plan inside the code 1 band, time to landing, souls on board and the plan of action added only after each item was prompted. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to state the pattern type and the method of stopping the A/C with the same precision as the other items.
texts_at.2: SP declared the emergency with a plan inside the code 2 band, correcting an omission of the souls on board and the plan of action identified without IP input. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to build the complete call before transmitting rather than completing it afterward.
texts_at.3: SP established the game plan first and then declared, giving ATC the nature of the emergency, the time to landing, the souls on board and the briefing of the plan of action, with the plan of action a little less specific than the rest of the call. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to bring that part of the call to the same specificity.

texts_above.1: SP declared the emergency with a plan, with time to landing, souls on board and the plan of action missing from the first transmission. SP corrected the trend after a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified an omission of the souls on board and the plan of action without IP input, restated the complete call to ATC and added the pattern to be flown and the stopping intention. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady content of the emergency declaration.
texts_above.3: SP established the game plan first and then declared, giving ATC the nature of the emergency, the time to landing, the souls on board and the briefing of the plan of action, with the pattern to be flown and the method of stopping the A/C both stated without prompting. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate content of the emergency declaration.
texts_above.4: SP declared with a complete plan and added the fuel remaining, the field selected and the point at which the plan would be changed if the situation deteriorated. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary content of the emergency declaration.

error_modes.label: Predetermined ejection decision point (Egress/Ejection step)
error_modes.source: technique:1.21 TABLETOP AND STAND-UP EMERGENCY PROCEDURES (EPS)

texts.0: SP did not review the Emergency Ground Egress and Controlled Ejection Checklists and did not determine at what point ejection would be initiated if the situation deteriorated. When the IP degraded the malfunction, SP continued to work through the checklists with no decision point in mind. The IP had to stop the exercise and teach the Egress and Ejection step of the method.
texts.1: SP stated that ejection would be considered if the situation worsened but produced the conditions and the altitude of that decision only after repeated prompting by the IP. Treatment of the Egress and Ejection step stayed at the minimum acceptable limit. Both checklists were reviewed, yet the decision point was defined by the IP and not by SP.
texts.2: SP passed from the declaration straight to following the plan and omitted the Egress and Ejection step. SP identified the omission without IP input, reviewed both checklists and stated the altitude and the conditions at which ejection would be initiated before continuing with the recovery.
texts.3: SP reviewed the Emergency Ground Egress and Controlled Ejection Checklists and stated in advance the conditions and the altitude at which ejection would be initiated. The decision point was consistent with the malfunction and with the recovery profile planned. The remainder of the exercise was flown against that predetermined criterion.
texts.4: SP reviewed both checklists and defined the ejection decision point together with every parameter that would trigger it, including the terrain along the planned track and the controllability limit accepted. When the IP degraded the situation, SP applied the criterion already stated without hesitation. The reasoning behind each parameter was explained correctly at the post-flight briefing.
texts.marginal: SP determined in advance when ejection would be initiated to the required standard, but the criterion was expressed as a single altitude, without reference to controllability or to the terrain along the planned recovery. The decision point was still usable. SP is expected to define the ejection criteria with all the conditions that would make ejection necessary.

texts_at.0: SP practiced defining the ejection decision point, with the IP prompting each action verbally as the item developed, this being SP's first presentation of the item. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point, and SP is expected to take over more of the sequence without prompting next time.
texts_at.1: SP determined in advance when ejection would be initiated inside the code 1 band, the conditions and altitude of that decision produced only after repeated prompting. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to define the ejection criteria with all the conditions that would make ejection necessary.
texts_at.2: SP determined in advance when ejection would be initiated inside the code 2 band, correcting an omitted Egress and Ejection step identified without IP input. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to include the step at the point it belongs in the sequence rather than after it has been skipped.
texts_at.3: SP reviewed the Emergency Ground Egress and Controlled Ejection Checklists and stated in advance the conditions and the altitude at which ejection would be initiated, with the criterion expressed as a single altitude rather than including controllability or terrain. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to add those references so the criterion is as complete as the rest of the plan.

texts_above.1: SP determined in advance when ejection would be initiated, with the conditions and altitude of that decision incomplete at the first briefing. The adjustment followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP identified an omitted Egress and Ejection step without IP input, reviewed both checklists and stated the altitude and conditions at which ejection would be initiated before continuing with the recovery. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable definition of the ejection decision point.
texts_above.3: SP reviewed the Emergency Ground Egress and Controlled Ejection Checklists and stated in advance the conditions and the altitude at which ejection would be initiated, consistent with the malfunction and the recovery profile planned. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good definition of the ejection decision point.
texts_above.4: SP reviewed both checklists and defined the ejection decision point together with every parameter that would trigger it, including the terrain along the planned track and the controllability limit accepted. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior definition of the ejection decision point.
